title: Bheeshma's Terrible Vow
body:
Bheeshma's Terrible Vow

When King Shantanu approached the chief of the fishermen to ask for Satyavati's hand in marriage, the astute chief placed a heavy condition: 'The child born of Satyavati must be crowned the king after you.' Shantanu, although mad with passion, could not make this promise, as it meant setting aside the godlike Devavrata, his eldest son, who was the rightful heir-apparent to the throne. Sick with baffled desire and pining away with secret sorrow, the king returned to Hastinapur in silence.
Noticing his father's declining health and silent anguish, Devavrata approached him and asked: 'My father, you have all that the heart could wish. Why then are you so unhappy? Why are you like one pining away with a secret sorrow?' Shantanu prevaricated, ashamed to reveal his lustful desire, and claimed that his anxiety was for the perpetuation of the family, as Devavrata was his only son and life in the world is uncertain.
Devavrata, determined to find the true cause of his father's grief, questioned the king's charioteer and learned of the ferryman's condition. He immediately went with a delegation of elders to the chief of the fishermen. In the presence of all, Devavrata made his first supreme renunciation: 'I give you my word that the son born of this maiden Satyavati shall be king, and I renounce in his favor my right as heir-apparent.'
The chief of the fishermen praised his heroism but raised a logical objection: 'O best of the Bharata race, I have no doubt you will keep your word. But how can I hope that the children born of you will renounce their birthright? Your sons will naturally be mighty heroes like you, and will be hard to resist if they seek to seize the kingdom by force. This is the doubt that torments me.'
Hearing this knotty question, Devavrata took his second, terrifying vow. Raising his arm to the heavens, he declared: 'I shall never marry, and I dedicate myself to a life of unbroken chastity (Brahmacharya).' As he uttered these words of absolute renunciation, the gods showered flowers on his head, and cries of 'Bheeshma! Bheeshma!' resounded in the air—meaning 'the one who undertakes a terrible vow and fulfills it.' Devavrata escorted Satyavati to his father's capital, where she was married to King Shantanu.
